GitHub fixes make_latest when the prerelease flag is WRITTEN and never recomputes it, so `gh release edit <tag> --prerelease=false` leaves /releases/latest where it was. repos/paiml/forjar/releases/latest resolved to v1.25.2 while v1.26.0, v1.27.0 and v1.28.0 were full releases days newer. Gate R now asks where that URL points, and a pointer that did not answer is judged against what the release IS.

systems: Homebrew (a formula's url is a versioned tarball; the 'latest' pointer is never what an install resolves)
rustup (channel manifests are published per-date and 'stable' is a written file, not a computed newest)
Debian archive (Release files name the version; 'latest' is a symlink an archive tool writes and dak verifies)
npm (dist-tags are explicit writes; `npm publish` sets `latest` unless --tag says otherwise, and `npm dist-tag ls` is the check)
crux.verdict: accept(every surveyed system treats 'latest' as a WRITTEN pointer that can disagree with the newest artifact, and every one of them has a way to read it back — npm's `dist-tag ls`, dak's verify, rustup's manifest fetch. GitHub is the same shape: make_latest is written when the prerelease flag is written. forjar had the write and not the read-back, which is exactly the gap that let the pointer sit four releases behind. Where forjar is WORSE than npm: the promotion is still an operator step, so this refuses a release that was not promoted rather than promoting it. Where it is better than Homebrew's model: the arm names both tags — the one being checked and the one the URL answers — so the reader is told which of the two is wrong.)
